summary: Defines a CoAP usage for RELOAD that helps federate wireless sensor networks in a peer-to-peer way. CoAP nodes can store resources in a RELOAD overlay, look them up, and use the overlay as a cache for sensor data.

eli5.summary: Many small sensors share their readings through a big shared bulletin board that no single computer runs.

subtitle: How sensor networks can find each other and share readings through a peer-to-peer overlay instead of a central server.

tldr.problem: Separate wireless sensor networks spread over a wide area need a way to find each other and share data without relying on centralized servers.
tldr.mechanism: CoAP nodes store a mapping from their CoAP URI to their Node-ID in a RELOAD overlay, look it up with a fetch, connect directly with AppAttach, and can cache sensor values in the overlay.
tldr.outcome: It defines two new RELOAD data Kinds, CoAP-REGISTRATION and CoAP-CACHING, and two new access control policies. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7650 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6940 (RELOAD) and RFC 7252 (CoAP).

sections.title: Why CoAP Needs RELOAD
sections.content:
This RFC defines a CoAP Usage for RELOAD. It lets CoAP nodes store resources in a RELOAD peer-to-peer overlay, gives them a lookup service, and lets them use the overlay as a cache for sensor data. All of this runs inside the overlay itself, without centralized servers.

The target is interconnected devices over a wide geographic area, for example several Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) that must be federated over a wider network. Those WSNs would connect through nodes that have long range modules (2G, 3G, 4G) as well as short range ones (XBee, ZigBee, Bluetooth LE).

The devices may differ at the radio layer, but the RFC expects them to share one application-layer protocol, CoAP (RFC 7252). RELOAD (RFC 6940) is an overlay network with pluggable application layers that reuse its forwarding, storage and lookup functions, and the CoAP Usage is one such layer.
sections.eli5: Lots of tiny sensors in different places need to find each other. Instead of one boss computer keeping the address book, all the computers in the group keep it together.

sections.title: Node Roles in the Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC extends the RELOAD roles of Client (no routing or storage duties) and Peer (can route for others) with Sensor, Actuator and Proxy Node roles. Physical devices can fill one or several roles.

Three kinds of node result:

  • A Constrained Node (CN) has limited computing power, is usually asleep to save battery, and is always a sensor or an actuator. A CN is not part of the RELOAD overlay, so it cannot act as a client, peer or proxy.
  • A RELOAD Node (RN) MUST implement client functionality and is often a full peer.
  • A Proxy Node (PN) MUST implement RN functionality and acts as a sink for the low-rate wireless network, connecting it to the wide area network or the Internet.
sections.eli5: Tiny sleepy sensors cannot join the big group themselves. Each one has a helper at the edge of its small network that talks to the big group for it.

sections.title: Registration and Lookup
sections.content:
CoAP URIs are normally resolved with DNS. In a RELOAD environment the overlay as a whole does that job. Instead of registering a URI, a peer stores a CoAPRegistration structure under a hash of its own URI, using the CoAP-REGISTRATION Kind-ID and a dictionary data model. The hash is usually SHA-1 in RELOAD.

In the RFC's example, a proxy with Node-ID 9996172 registers four sensors under coap://overlay-1.com/proxy-1/.well-known/, described in the CoRE link format of RFC 6690. A node that wants to know what proxy-1 serves performs a fetch in the overlay using the SHA-1 hash of that URI. The result gives the Node-ID of the responsible RN and the set of URIs needed to read the CNs behind it.

Because the data model is a dictionary, several nodes can store under the same Resource-ID. In the example, peers 9996172 and 9996173 both store temperature links under coap://overlay-1.com/temperature/.well-known/, so one fetch returns both.
sections.eli5: Each helper writes its name and a list of its sensors on the shared bulletin board under a label. Anyone who looks up the label finds who to ask and what they can ask for.

sections.title: Connecting and Reading Data
sections.content:
After the lookup, the requesting RN sends a RELOAD AppAttach request to the Node-ID it obtained. After the AppAttach negotiation, it can read the sensors using the information from the lookup, for example GET /sensors/temp-1.

The RFC's Figure 3 shows the full sequence: a RELOAD Fetch request and answer, an AppAttach request and answer relayed through the overlay, ICE connectivity checks, and then a CoAP confirmable GET that the proxy forwards to the sensor and answers with an ACK 200.
sections.eli5: Once you know who to ask, you call them directly and ask for the reading you want.

sections.title: Caching Sensor Data in the Overlay
sections.content:
CoAP already allows caching in CoAP proxies. This RFC adds a second mechanism that stores sensor information directly in the overlay. It is meant mainly for CNs with sensors, because their batteries force them to sleep for long periods.

When a CN wakes up, it sends its latest readings to its proxy, which stores them in the overlay as a RELOAD StoredData structure (RFC 6940) using the SingleValue format. The stored data value is a CoAPCaching structure that holds either a ProxyCache or a SensorCache.

  • A ProxyCache holds the proxy's Node-ID and a list of SensorEntry items, each with the sensor's CoAP URI, its sensor_info and its values.
  • A SensorCache holds the information and cached values of only one sensor. Its CoAP URI is not needed because it is the one used to build the Resource-ID.
  • A SensorValue carries measurement_time (milliseconds since midnight Jan 1, 1970 UTC), lifetime (validity in milliseconds since the measurement time) and an opaque value.
sections.eli5: While a sensor naps, its latest reading stays pinned on the bulletin board, so people can read it without waking the sensor.

sections.title: The Two New Kinds and Their Access Rules
sections.content:
Section 8 defines the CoAP-REGISTRATION Kind (dictionary data model, keyed by the Node-ID of the storing RN, so each RN stores one mapping) and the CoAP-CACHING Kind (single value). For both, the resource name is the CoAP URI.

RELOAD requires every storable Kind to have an access control policy, and none of the base policies fit, so this RFC defines two. Under URI-MATCH, a value MUST be written and overwritten if and only if the signer's certificate has a uniformResourceIdentifier entry in its subjectAltName extension that, in canonical form, hashes to the Resource-ID. URI-NODE-MATCH adds that the dictionary key equals the Node-ID in the certificate and is the one in the SignerIdentity cert_hash. REGISTRATION uses URI-NODE-MATCH and CACHING uses URI-MATCH, and the coap: prefix is removed before matching.
sections.eli5: Only the owner of an address label may write on it. The rules check the owner's ID card before letting anyone change the board.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of RELOAD and CoAP apply, and implementations MUST follow all security rules of both specifications. RELOAD relies on public key certificates for signing messages and stored objects, and can use TLS or DTLS at the connection level.

A CoAP node that advertises itself through this mechanism is more likely to be attacked than a node (especially a sleepy one) that does not. The caching mechanism is additional to CoAP's own caching, and the peer storing the data is responsible for validating the signature on it.

IANA assigned Kind-ID 0x105 to CoAP-REGISTRATION and 0x106 to CoAP-CACHING, and created a registry of access control policies containing URI-NODE-MATCH and URI-MATCH.
sections.eli5: Everything on the board is signed, so people can tell who wrote it. Telling the world where your sensor lives also makes it easier for bad guys to find.
